title: A Gallery of Signals
intro: Every signal in the viewer, walked through from the signal to its transform, poles and zeros, region of convergence, response on the imaginary axis, and stability. The page ends with the bridge from the s-plane to the z-plane.

blocks.text: Each section below goes through one input of the viewer the way its Next step button does: the signal, the transform and its region, the surface, the response along the axis, and what that says about stability. The viewer under each heading is set to that signal. Decay rate a is $0.5$ and Frequency ω₀ is $1.5$ unless stated; every number can be checked against the formula beside it.
The unit impulse

items: Signal (unit impulse δ(t)): $x(t) = \delta(t)$, one unit of area at $t = 0$.
Transform: $X(s) = 1$, ROC the whole plane. No poles, no zeros.
Surface: a flat sheet at height 1 (0 dB) over the whole plane.
Axis: $|X(j\omega)| = 1$ at every frequency. An impulse contains every frequency equally; it is the signal a filter's frequency response is measured with.
Stability: the integral of $|x|$ is 1, finite, and the axis is in the region. Causal.

blocks.text: The response panel is a flat line at 0 dB, the middle of its height range. Nothing moves when you drag Probe frequency ω. Tilt to 85° and the contour map has no features at all.
The delayed impulse

items: Signal (delayed impulse δ(t−1)): $x(t) = \delta(t-1)$, an impulse at $t = 1$.
Transform: $X(s) = e^{-s}$, ROC the whole plane. No poles, no zeros.
Surface: a smooth ramp with $|X| = e^{-\sigma}$: height $2.72$ at $\sigma = -1$ and $0.368$ at $\sigma = 1$, in decibels a straight ramp of $-8.69$ dB per unit of $\sigma$.
Axis: $|X(j\omega)| = 1$ at every frequency (0 dB); the delay only changes the phase, by $-\omega$.
Stability: stable and causal. The only difference from the plain impulse is a tilt of the surface away from the axis.

blocks.text: Compare with the unit impulse: on the imaginary axis the two are indistinguishable, and the delay shows only in the tilt of the 3D surface. The viewer's step on the surface says there is no ruler reading, since $e^{-s}$ is not a ratio of polynomials.
The unit step

items: Signal (unit step u(t)): $x(t) = 1$ for $t \ge 0$.
Transform: $X(s) = 1/s$, ROC $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. A pole at the origin.
Surface: a single peak at the origin, falling away as $1/|s|$. Solid to the right of the axis, faded to the left.
Axis: $|X(j\omega)| = 1/\omega$: $2$ at $\omega = 0.5$, $1$ at 1, $0.5$ at 2 and $0.333$ at 3; the pole sits at the start of the axis and the response is unbounded there.
Stability: the axis is the edge of the region, so the Fourier transform exists only in a limiting sense. Causal, but not BIBO stable: a steady input would make the output grow without limit.

blocks.text: The shaded region in the s-plane panel is the right half-plane, with its edge on the imaginary axis. Slide Probe frequency ω from 3 toward 0: the response panel rises as $1/\omega$, $-9.54$ dB at 3 and $+6.02$ dB at $0.5$, and the violet line from the origin to the probe is the one distance that matters.
The decaying exponential

items: Signal (decaying exponential e^(−at)u(t)): $x(t) = e^{-at}$ for $t \ge 0$.
Transform: $X(s) = 1/(s+a)$, ROC $\operatorname{Re} s > -a$. One pole at $-a$.
Surface: one peak over the pole, solid on its right. For $a = 0.5$ the height at the origin is $2$ ($6.02$ dB).
Axis: $|X(j\omega)| = 1/\sqrt{a^2 + \omega^2}$, largest at $\omega = 0$ and down 3 dB at $\omega = a$. A low-pass response: $0.894$ at $\omega = 1$, $0.329$ at 3.
Stability: stable and causal for $a > 0$. At $a = 0$ it is the step, and for $a < 0$ the pole is on the right and the signal grows.

blocks.text: Drag Decay rate a below zero, to $-0.5$: the pole crosses the axis, the signal panel turns into a growing exponential, the shaded region no longer contains the axis, and the last walk-through step reports instability.
The left-sided exponential

items: Signal (left-sided exponential −e^(−at)u(−t)): $x(t) = -e^{-at}$ for $t < 0$ and $0$ after.
Transform: $X(s) = 1/(s+a)$ again, but ROC $\operatorname{Re} s < -a$.
Surface: the same landscape as the decaying exponential, solid on the left of the pole and faded on the right.
Axis: for $a = 0.5$ the axis is in the faded part, so the formula's slice $1/\sqrt{a^2+\omega^2}$ is not the Fourier transform of anything here: the signal grows as $t \to -\infty$.
Stability: not causal, and unstable for $a > 0$. For $a < 0$ the region contains the axis, and then it is stable (and still not causal).

blocks.text: Switch Input signal between this and the decaying exponential and watch only the shading flip: the surface, the poles and the response curve stay put. That is the whole point of the region of convergence.
The two-sided exponential

items: Signal (two-sided exponential e^(−a|t|)): $x(t) = e^{-a|t|}$ for every $t$.
Transform: $X(s) = 2a/(a^2 - s^2)$, ROC $-a < \operatorname{Re} s < a$. Poles at $\pm a$.
Surface: two peaks, mirror images through the imaginary axis, with the solid strip between them; $|X(0)| = 4$ at $a = 0.5$.
Axis: $|X(j\omega)| = 2a/(a^2 + \omega^2)$, which is $4$ at $\omega = 0$ ($12.0$ dB), $0.8$ at $\omega = 1$ and falls like $1/\omega^2$ at high frequency.
Stability: stable (the axis is inside the strip), not causal. For $a \le 0$ there is no region at all.

blocks.text: Push Decay rate a to 0 and the strip closes: the viewer says there is no region of convergence and fades the whole surface.
The ramped exponential

items: Signal (ramped exponential t·e^(−at)u(t)): $x(t) = t\,e^{-at}$ for $t \ge 0$.
Transform: $X(s) = 1/(s+a)^2$, ROC $\operatorname{Re} s > -a$. A double pole at $-a$.
Surface: one peak steeper than a single pole's; in decibels a double pole rises twice as fast. $|X(0)| = 4$ ($12.0$ dB) at $a = 0.5$.
Axis: $|X(j\omega)| = 1/(a^2 + \omega^2)$: $4$ at $\omega = 0$, $0.8$ at $\omega = 1$. It falls 12 dB per doubling of frequency at the top end, twice as fast as a single pole.
Stability: the signal rises to $1/(ae) = 0.736$ at $t = 2$ and then dies away. Stable and causal for $a > 0$.

blocks.text: The signal panel shows the hump: zero at the start, peak at $t = 1/a$, decay after. The s-plane panel marks the pole $\times 2$.
The damped cosine

items: Signal (damped cosine e^(−at)cos(ω₀t)u(t)): $x(t) = e^{-at}\cos(\omega_0 t)$ for $t \ge 0$.
Transform: $X(s) = (s+a)/\bigl((s+a)^2 + \omega_0^2\bigr)$, ROC $\operatorname{Re} s > -a$. Poles at $-a \pm j\omega_0$ and a zero at $-a$.
Surface: two peaks above and below the real axis and a pit between them on the real axis at the zero.
Axis: $|X(j\omega)|$ is $0.2$ at $\omega = 0$, $0.620$ at 1, $1.040$ at $1.5$ and $0.425$ at 3: a resonance near $\omega_0$ that does not start from zero.
Stability: stable and causal for $a > 0$. At the start it equals 1, which the initial value theorem confirms: $sX \to 1$.

blocks.text: Drag Decay rate a to 0.1: the poles close in on the axis and the peak of the response panel at $\omega \approx 1.5$ climbs, while the zero at $-0.1$ follows the poles' $\sigma$.
The damped sine

items: Signal (damped sine e^(−at)sin(ω₀t)u(t)): $x(t) = e^{-at}\sin(\omega_0 t)$ for $t \ge 0$.
Transform: $X(s) = \omega_0/\bigl((s+a)^2 + \omega_0^2\bigr)$, ROC $\operatorname{Re} s > -a$. The same poles as the cosine and no zero.
Surface: the cosine's two peaks without the pit. At the origin the height is $0.6$.
Axis: a resonance with its peak at $\sqrt{\omega_0^2 - a^2} = 1.414$ and height exactly $1.00$; $0.832$ at $\omega = 1$ and $0.209$ at 3.
Stability: stable and causal; starts at $x(0) = 0$ and has its first peak $0.626$ at $t = 0.833$ s.

blocks.text: With the sine and the cosine selected in turn, notice that the two surfaces differ only near the real axis: the poles that make the ringing are common, and the numerator decides how the ringing is started.
The 3-second pulse

items: Signal (3-second pulse u(t)−u(t−3)): $x(t) = 1$ for $0 \le t < 3$ and $0$ elsewhere.
Transform: $X(s) = (1 - e^{-3s})/s$, ROC the whole plane. No poles. Zeros on the imaginary axis at $\omega = 2\pi k/3$, that is $\pm 2.09$, $\pm 4.19$, ...
Surface: a mound with $X(0) = 3$ (the area, $9.54$ dB), climbing steeply on the left and dropping on the right, because of the $e^{-3s}$ factor.
Axis: a ripple that dives to zero at $\omega = 2.09$, the first of the zeros, and returns, with smaller lobes between zeros.
Stability: stable and causal. It has no poles at all; a finite signal is as tame as a signal can be.

blocks.text: Sweep ω: the response panel dips to the floor at $2.09$ rad/s, where $\omega T = 2\pi$ for the pulse's duration $T = 3$ s: a sinusoid of exactly one cycle per 3 seconds adds to zero over the pulse.
The notch filter

items: Signal (notch filter): $X(s) = (s^2 + \omega_0^2)/(s^2 + 0.75\,s + \omega_0^2)$ for $\omega_0 = 1.5$; as a signal, an impulse at $t = 0$ minus a decaying oscillation.
Transform: zeros at $\pm j1.5$ on the axis, poles at $-0.375 \pm j1.452$, ROC $\operatorname{Re} s > -0.375$.
Surface: a pit in the axis directly beside a pole peak, on each side of the real axis.
Axis: $1$ at $\omega = 0$, $0.859$ at 1, $0.266$ at $1.4$, exactly $0$ at $1.5$, $0.759$ at 2 and $0.949$ at 3: unity gain everywhere but a narrow notch.
Stability: stable and causal, since the poles are on the left. It is a filter, not a signal; its impulse response begins with an impulse.

blocks.text: Set Probe frequency ω to 1.5 and the response panel plunges to the floor. Drag Frequency ω₀ to 1 and the notch, with its zeros and poles, moves down the axis to $\omega = 1$.
From the s-plane to the z-plane

Sample a continuous signal every $T$ seconds and the exponential $e^{-at}$ becomes $e^{-anT} = (e^{-aT})^n$: the discrete signal $r^n$ with $r = e^{-aT}$. A pole at $s = p$ in the s-plane becomes a pole at $z = e^{pT}$ in the z-plane. Writing $s = \sigma + j\omega$,

blocks.tex: z = e^{sT} = e^{\sigma T}\, e^{j\omega T}, \qquad |z| = e^{\sigma T}, \quad \angle z = \omega T

items: The left half-plane, $\sigma < 0$, maps inside the unit circle, $|z| < 1$. Stable continuous poles become stable discrete poles. A point at $\sigma = 0.5$ with $T = 1$ lands at radius $e^{0.5} = 1.65$, outside.
The imaginary axis, $\sigma = 0$, maps onto the unit circle, $|z| = 1$. So the Fourier transform (the axis) becomes the discrete-time Fourier transform (the circle).
The right half-plane maps outside the circle.

A horizontal strip of height $2\pi/T$ covers the whole z-plane once. Frequencies $\omega$ and $\omega + 2\pi/T$ land on the same point: this is aliasing. With $T = 1$, the frequencies $1.5$ and $1.5 + 2\pi = 7.78$ rad/s give the same $z = e^{j1.5}$.

blocks.text: As a worked example take the decaying exponential's pole at $s = -0.5$ with $T = 1$: it lands at $z = e^{-0.5} = 0.607$, so $e^{-0.5t}u(t)$ sampled at $t = n$ is $0.607^n u[n]$. The damped sine's poles at $-0.5 \pm j1.5$ land at $0.607\,e^{\pm j1.5}$, radius $0.607$ and angle $1.5$ rad $= 85.9^\circ$. With a faster sampling, $T = 0.1$ s, the same poles land at radius $e^{-0.05} = 0.951$ and angle $0.15$ rad $= 8.59^\circ$: closer to $z = 1$ and to the unit circle. The faster you sample, the more the poles bunch near $z = 1$, which is how the unit circle ends up looking like the axis for low frequencies. The Z-Transform topic, The Z-Transform (#/math/z-transform), has the matching gallery: A Gallery of Signals (#/math/z-transform/gallery).
Cheat sheet

items: $\delta(t) \leftrightarrow 1$, every $s$; $\delta(t - T) \leftrightarrow e^{-sT}$.
$u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/s$, $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.
$e^{-at}u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/(s+a)$, $\operatorname{Re} s > -a$; $-e^{-at}u(-t) \leftrightarrow 1/(s+a)$, $\operatorname{Re} s < -a$.
$e^{-a|t|} \leftrightarrow 2a/(a^2 - s^2)$, $-a < \operatorname{Re} s < a$.
$t\,e^{-at}u(t) \leftrightarrow 1/(s+a)^2$, $\operatorname{Re} s > -a$.
$e^{-at}\cos(\omega_0 t)u(t) \leftrightarrow (s+a)/\bigl((s+a)^2 + \omega_0^2\bigr)$; the sine has $\omega_0$ on top instead.
$u(t) - u(t - T) \leftrightarrow (1 - e^{-sT})/s$, every $s$.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Match the surface
blocks.text: A surface has a single peak on the negative real axis at $\sigma = -2$, no pit, solid to the right of the pole, and a height of $0.5$ at $s = 0$. Which signal is it, and how far does the response fall between $\omega = 0$ and $\omega = 2$?
solution: One pole at $-2$, no zeros, right-sided: $X(s) = 1/(s+2)$, the signal $e^{-2t}u(t)$. The height at the origin is $1/2$, as stated. At $\omega = 2$ the distance to the pole is $\sqrt{4 + 4} = 2.83$, so $|X| = 0.354$, which is $-3.01$ dB: the response has fallen by 3 dB at the corner, as for any single pole.

blocks.title: Into the z-plane
blocks.text: A continuous system has poles at $-1 \pm j2$. Where are its poles after sampling at $T = 0.5$ s, and is the discrete system stable?
solution: $z = e^{sT}$ with $s = -1 \pm j2$ and $T = 0.5$: radius $e^{-0.5} = 0.607$, angle $\pm 2 \times 0.5 = \pm 1$ rad $= \pm 57.3^\circ$. The radius is under 1, so the poles are inside the unit circle: stable, as expected from the left half-plane.
blocks.answer: $0.607\,e^{\pm j1}$, inside the unit circle: stable.
